title: Every Drop Counts: Saving Water in Saudi Arabia
passage:
Imagine a huge country that has no permanent rivers or lakes at all. That country is Saudi Arabia, where much of the land is desert, rainfall is rare and summers are extremely hot. Nevertheless, millions of people depend on a reliable supply of water every day for drinking, cooking, washing and growing food. Where does all this water come from, and how can we make sure that enough remains for the future?

The Kingdom obtains its water from two main sources. The first is groundwater, which is stored deep beneath the surface in layers of rock and sand known as aquifers. Some of this water collected thousands of years ago, when the climate of Arabia was much wetter, so once it has been used, it cannot easily be replaced. The second source is the sea, because large factories called desalination plants remove the salt from seawater so that people can drink it safely. In fact, Saudi Arabia is one of the largest producers of desalinated water in the world.

However, desalination is expensive. The process needs a great deal of energy, and the extremely salty water that remains afterwards must be returned to the sea carefully to protect marine life. Pumping groundwater from deep wells is also costly, and it gradually empties these ancient underground stores. This is exactly why conserving water matters so much: every litre that we waste had to be found, purified and carried to our homes.

Agriculture consumes the largest share of water in the Kingdom. For this reason, many farmers now rely on drip irrigation, a system of narrow pipes that delivers small drops of water directly to the roots of plants. Because very little water is lost to evaporation, this method uses far less water than flooding entire fields. In addition, several cities treat used water from homes and reuse it to irrigate parks and gardens.

Families can contribute as well. A national programme called "Qatrah," which means "a drop," encourages everyone to use water responsibly, since simple habits can make a significant difference. Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth. Take shorter showers instead of baths, and repair dripping taps promptly, because a single leaking tap can waste thousands of litres in a year. Water plants early in the morning or in the evening, when less water evaporates in the fierce heat of the sun.

Conserving water is also part of our values, since the Holy Qur'an teaches us to eat and drink without being wasteful. How wonderful it would be if every family in the Kingdom saved just a few buckets a day! Together, these small drops could become an ocean of savings for the generations to come.

questions.stem: Which word is closest in meaning to “obtains” as it is used in paragraph 2?
options: loses
gets
stores
cleans
questions.why: The Kingdom “obtains” its water from two sources, meaning it gets its water from them.

questions.stem: Which word is the opposite of “promptly” as it is used in paragraph 5?
options: quickly
carefully
often
late
questions.why: “Promptly” means quickly and without delay; its opposite is “late”. “Quickly” is a synonym, not an opposite.

questions.stem: Read this sentence from paragraph 4: “Because very little water is lost to evaporation, this method uses far less water than flooding entire fields.” What does “evaporation” mean?
options: water turning into vapour in the air
water soaking deep into the ground
water flowing back into the sea
water being cleaned so it can be reused
questions.why: Paragraph 5 adds that less water “evaporates in the fierce heat of the sun”, so evaporation is water turning into vapour in the heat.

questions.stem: Which word from paragraph 4 is a verb?
options: narrow
directly
delivers
system
questions.why: “Delivers” is an action; “narrow” is an adjective, “directly” an adverb and “system” a noun.

questions.stem: Which plural noun from the text does NOT end in -s?
options: people
layers
plants
families
questions.why: “People” is an irregular plural of “person”; the others are regular plurals.

questions.stem: Which word belongs to the same word family as “conserving”?
options: conversation
conservation
construction
consonant
questions.why: “Conservation” shares the root and meaning of “conserve”; “conversation” only looks similar.

questions.stem: Use the word “significant” in a meaningful sentence of your own.
questions.model: Reading for twenty minutes every evening made a significant difference to my vocabulary by the end of the year.
rubric: 2 = a complete, correct sentence that uses “significant” with its meaning (large or important enough to be noticed)
1 = the word is used correctly but the sentence is incomplete or has several errors
0 = the word is missing, misused, or the sentence copies the text
questions.why: “Significant” means large or important enough to have an effect.

questions.stem: What is the plural of “supply”, which appears in paragraph 1?
options: supplys
suppleys
supply's
supplies
questions.why: A consonant + y changes y to -ies: supply → supplies.

questions.stem: What type of sentence is “Imagine a huge country that has no permanent rivers or lakes at all.”?
options: a question
an exclamation
a command
a statement
questions.why: It begins with the verb “Imagine” and tells the reader to do something, so it is a command.

questions.stem: Which is another suitable title for the whole text?
options: Every Drop Matters in a Dry Land
How Desalination Plants Are Built
The History of Farming in Arabia
Rivers and Lakes of the Kingdom
questions.why: The text explains why water is precious in a desert country and how to save it. Desalination is only one part, and the country has no rivers.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the text?
options: to tell the story of one farming family in the desert
to compare Saudi Arabia with countries that have rivers
to explain how to dig a deep well safely
to inform readers about water and encourage them to save it
questions.why: It gives facts about water sources and costs, then urges families to save water.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea of paragraph 3?
options: Desalination plants always destroy marine life in the sea.
Producing fresh water is costly, so wasting it is a serious problem.
Groundwater is much cheaper to use than desalinated water.
Deep wells are easy to dig and can never be emptied.
questions.why: Paragraph 3 explains the costs of desalination and pumping and ends: “This is exactly why conserving water matters so much.”

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, why can some groundwater not easily be replaced?
options: It is too salty for people to drink.
Desalination plants use all of it.
It collected thousands of years ago, when Arabia was wetter.
It is stored underneath the sea.
questions.why: The water was collected when the climate was much wetter, and today's rare rain cannot refill it quickly.

questions.stem: Which genre best describes this text?
options: expository nonfiction
a short story
a poem
a biography
questions.why: It explains a real topic with facts, causes and solutions; it has no characters or plot.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 4, why does drip irrigation use far less water than flooding fields?
options: It only works at night.
It uses seawater instead of groundwater.
Farmers use it only once a year.
Very little water is lost to evaporation.
questions.why: The paragraph says: “Because very little water is lost to evaporation, this method uses far less water.”

questions.stem: Which topic does the writer discuss BEFORE explaining drip irrigation?
options: water-saving habits for families
the costs of desalination and pumping
the meaning of “Qatrah”
the teaching of the Holy Qur'an
questions.why: The costs come in paragraph 3; drip irrigation is in paragraph 4, and the other topics come later.

questions.stem: In paragraph 5, how does the writer speak directly to the reader?
options: by telling a story about the writer's family
by quoting a farmer's opinion
by giving commands such as “Turn off the tap”
by asking readers to write a letter
questions.why: Sentences such as “Turn off the tap” and “Take shorter showers” tell the reader what to do.

questions.stem: According to paragraph 2, what are aquifers?
options: layers of rock and sand that store water underground
factories that remove salt from seawater
narrow pipes used to water plants
deep wells used for pumping water
questions.why: Groundwater is stored “in layers of rock and sand known as aquifers.”

questions.stem: Using paragraphs 2 and 3, why are the ancient underground stores slowly becoming empty?
options: Desalination plants make the water salty.
Sand from the desert fills them up.
The sea pushes the water away from the land.
Water is pumped out but cannot easily be replaced.
questions.why: Paragraph 2 says used groundwater cannot easily be replaced, and paragraph 3 says pumping gradually empties the stores.

questions.stem: In your opinion, why does the writer end paragraph 1 with a question?
options: to show that nobody knows where water comes from
to make readers curious about the answers that follow
to test whether readers already know the facts
to change the topic before paragraph 2
questions.why: The question “Where does all this water come from…?” is answered in the rest of the text, so it draws the reader on.

questions.stem: Which words best describe the writer's attitude toward saving water?
options: serious but hopeful
careless and bored
angry and unkind
unsure and confused
questions.why: The writer explains a serious problem (paragraph 3) but ends hopefully: small drops “could become an ocean of savings.”

questions.stem: How is drip irrigation different from flooding fields?
options: Flooding loses much less water to evaporation than drip irrigation does.
Drip irrigation uses seawater, while flooding uses only groundwater.
Drip irrigation sends water straight to the roots; flooding covers the whole field.
Both methods use exactly the same amount of water on a farm.
questions.why: Paragraph 4: drip irrigation “delivers small drops of water directly to the roots” and uses far less water than flooding.

questions.stem: What is the effect of repairing a dripping tap promptly?
options: It refills the underground aquifers.
It can save thousands of litres of water a year.
It makes tap water cleaner to drink.
It reduces the heat of the sun.
questions.why: Paragraph 5 says a single leaking tap can waste thousands of litres in a year.

questions.stem: Using paragraphs 2 and 3, what do desalinated water and groundwater have in common?
options: Both come from the sea.
Both can be replaced easily.
Both are used only by farmers.
Both are costly to provide.
questions.why: Desalination “is expensive”, and “pumping groundwater from deep wells is also costly.”

questions.stem: In your opinion, how does the writer make the information easy to follow?
options: It moves from the problem, to the sources and costs, then to solutions.
It follows one family through a whole day.
It repeats the same fact in every paragraph.
It gives numbers without any explanation.
questions.why: The paragraphs move in a clear order: the problem, the sources, the costs, then solutions for farms and families.

questions.stem: What does the expression “an ocean of savings” mean in paragraph 6?
options: a new sea that people will build
money kept in a bank by the beach
a very large amount of saved water
salty water from desalination plants
questions.why: It is figurative: many small drops saved by families add up to a huge amount.

questions.stem: Which sentence from the text is exclamatory?
options: Where does all this water come from, and how can we make sure that enough remains for the future?
How wonderful it would be if every family in the Kingdom saved just a few buckets a day!
Turn off the tap while you brush your teeth.
However, desalination is expensive.
questions.why: It expresses strong feeling and ends with an exclamation mark.

questions.stem: In your opinion, which is the BEST use of water in a desert country, according to the text's ideas?
options: washing the car with a running hose every day
filling a bath for a quick wash
watering the garden at noon
using drip irrigation to grow vegetables
questions.why: Drip irrigation grows food with little water; watering at noon loses more water to evaporation.

questions.stem: What most likely made the writer write this text?
options: a wish to sell more bottled water
a love of stories about the sea
concern that the Kingdom's water is limited and costly
a plan to build new swimming pools
questions.why: The writer stresses that water is scarce and expensive to produce and must not be wasted.

questions.stem: Which feeling is most present in the text?
options: responsibility
jealousy
boredom
anger
questions.why: The writer asks farmers, cities and families to take responsibility for saving water.

questions.stem: In your opinion, which information in the text is the LEAST clear?
options: the meaning of the word “Qatrah”
how cities treat used water before reusing it
why desalination is expensive
what drip irrigation is
questions.why: The writer says cities treat used water but never explains how; the other points are explained.

questions.stem: Which of the following events could really happen?
options: A great river suddenly appears in the desert and flows forever.
Seawater becomes sweet by itself overnight without any plant.
A family uses less water by fixing leaks and taking short showers.
One tap supplies every home in the Kingdom with water.
questions.why: Fixing leaks and taking short showers are real habits named in the text.

questions.stem: Which title best describes the ideas in the text?
options: The Rainy Kingdom
Rivers of the Desert
Water Never Runs Out
Every Drop Counts
questions.why: The text shows that even small amounts of saved water add up.

questions.stem: Suggest a different ending for the text: write two or three sentences that add one more solution for saving water at school and explain why it would work.
questions.model: Schools could collect the water that drips from air-conditioning units and use it to irrigate the school garden. Because this water would otherwise be wasted, the garden would stay green without using fresh water from the taps. Students could also form a “water team” that checks the taps every week and reports any leaks.
rubric: 2 = a clear new ending with a sensible, realistic water-saving solution and a reason linked to the text
1 = an ending is given but the solution is unclear, unrealistic or not explained
0 = no answer, or the original ending is copied
questions.why: Any sensible, explained water-saving idea that fits the text's message is acceptable.

questions.stem: How can a school help to save water, using ideas from the text?
options: Put up signs reminding students to turn off taps.
Repair leaking taps promptly.
Water the school garden in the evening.
All of the above
questions.why: All three ideas match the advice in paragraph 5.
